Unlike plain‐text files (`*.txt`, `*.md`, etc.), you can’t just run `cat` on it and see readable text because the file is stored in a proprietary binary format.

To work with the contents you have a few options:

| What you want to do | How to proceed |
|---------------------|---------------|

| **Extract the Word XML** | Use `unzip -p MonthlySummary.docx word/document.xml > temp.xml`. Then you can pipe `temp.xml` through `sed` / `awk` / `grep` to pull out `<w:t>` elements (the actual text) before sorting. |
| **Convert to plain text** | Install a conversion tool like *pandoc* or *libreoffice --convert-to txt *.docx*, then apply `sort`. |

```bash
# Extract the main document XML
unzip -p MonthlySummary.docx word/document.xml > tmp_doc.xml

# Pull out the visible text nodes (<w:t>) and strip surrounding markup
grep '<w:t>' tmp_doc.xml \
    | sed -E 's/<[^>]+>//g' \   # removes tags
    | tr '\n\r' ' '            # collapse paragraphs into single line per paragraph
    | awk '{print $0}'         # keep each paragraph separate

# Now sort the resulting lines alphabetically
... | sort
```

That chain gives you a clean, alphabetical listing of the textual content inside the Word file.

If you’re okay with seeing the entire XML structure (which includes formatting tags), simply open the file in a text editor that supports viewing binary or zipped archives—most modern editors let you “Open Archive” or “Unpack”.
